book_title: Chapter 3: Follow the Sales Rupee — Supply Chain, Working Capital & Unit Economics
question: How do Azad Engineering's direct OEM distribution model, imported superalloy supply chain, and Tuniki Bollaram plants convert ₹100 of FY26 revenue into operating profit—and why does that ₹100 turn negative by the time it reaches free cash flow?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an engineering opinion; cash flow is the working-capital reality of how long your alloys sit on the shop floor and how fast your customer pays.
epigraph.author: Industrial Forensic Principle

web_blocks.title: Direct B2B OEM Distribution & Long-Term Supply Agreements

web_blocks.html: Azad Engineering has zero distributor or retail layers. Distribution is 100% direct B2B under multi-year Long-Term Contract and Price Agreements (LTCPAs). Global OEMs across Europe, Japan, and North America drive ~93% of sales, while domestic defence and power PSUs add ~7% [3][4][5]. Rather than bidding on spot tenders each quarter, Azad works under 4-to-8-year rate contracts. These agreements set part numbers, quality rules, annual volume bands, and raw-material indexation clauses upfront [5][12]. Between March 2025 and September 2026, Azad opened 44,800 sq. m. of customer-exclusive bays at Tuniki Bollaram [16][17]. Once a part is qualified in a dedicated bay, purchase orders flow from the OEM's global ERP straight into Azad's schedule.

web_blocks.title: Raw Material Sourcing, Hyderabad Footprint & The DSO/Inventory Cycle

web_blocks.html: Specialized raw materials come mostly from OEM-approved overseas mills [6]. These include certified nickel-based superalloys (Inconel, Waspaloy), titanium bar stock, and precision forgings. That creates a long supply-chain pipeline. Stock moves through ocean transit, customs clearance, and incoming lab checks before 5-axis machining. Parts then undergo NADCAP heat treatment, NDT, and final OEM sign-off before export dispatch. On the collection side, global OEMs enforce long export credit terms. Standalone debtor days sit in the 170–189 day range, reaching 189 days in FY26 [1][6]. Inventory days also spiked from 1,085 days in FY25 to 2,067 days in FY26. Azad stocked work-in-progress (WIP) and raw material across six new plants undergoing delta qualification [1][7]. To pull debtor days toward ~90 days, management is using bill discounting facilities (via ICICI Bank and DP World). It is also negotiating 50% advance payments on select OEM orders, though that raises finance costs [6][18].

The deterministic waterfall below scales audited consolidated FY26 (Mar 2026) P&L and cash-flow lines down to ₹100.00 of revenue. It starts from ₹603.00 Cr of consolidated sales [1] and reconciles disclosed standalone costs [14] to consolidated operating expenses.

notes.revenue: Audited FY26 consolidated revenue from operations: ₹603.00 Cr (+32% YoY) [1].
notes.cogs: Disclosed FY26 cost of materials consumed: ₹57.04 Cr (~9.5% of consolidated sales) [14].
notes.employee_cost: Disclosed FY26 employee benefits expense: ₹131.02 Cr (skilled machinists & engineering ramp) [14].
notes.other_opex: Other operating expenses (₹184.56 Cr standalone [14] + ₹5.38 Cr subsidiary/consolidation delta = ₹189.94 Cr) to match ₹378.00 Cr consolidated expenses [1].
notes.ebitda: Audited FY26 consolidated operating profit: ₹225.00 Cr (37.31% OPM) [1].
notes.da: Audited FY26 depreciation & amortization: ₹53.00 Cr (rising with Tuniki Bollaram plant commissioning) [1].
notes.interest: Finance costs: ₹31.00 Cr (up from ₹18.00 Cr in FY25 due to working capital & bill discounting) [1][6].
notes.other_income: Treasury & non-operating income (QIP cash deployment & FX): ₹46.00 Cr [1].
notes.pbt: Audited FY26 Profit Before Tax: ₹187.00 Cr [1].
notes.tax: Implied corporate tax expense (28.3% effective rate): ₹53.00 Cr [1].
notes.pat: Audited FY26 consolidated Net Profit: ₹134.00 Cr (22.22% net margin) [1].
notes.working_capital: Net working-capital & non-cash absorption (-₹306.00 Cr): debtor days 189 & inventory days 2,067 [1].
notes.cfo: Audited FY26 Cash Flow from Operations: -₹119.00 Cr (-31% CFO/EBITDA) [1].
notes.capex: Implied FY26 Capex (CFO -₹119.00 Cr less FCF -₹691.00 Cr = ₹572.00 Cr) for dedicated OEM plants [1].
notes.fcf: Audited FY26 Free Cash Flow: -₹691.00 Cr (funded by QIP cash & borrowings) [1][8].

web_blocks.caption: AZAD: Worked ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Audited Consolidated FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: Azad converts ₹100 of FY26 revenue into ₹37.31 of Operating EBITDA and ₹22.22 of accounting Net Profit, but working-capital absorption (-₹50.75 per ₹100) and plant capex (-₹94.86 per ₹100) turn Free Cash Flow to -₹114.59 per ₹100 of sales [1].

web_blocks.title: The Unit-Economics Paradox: Elite Margin, Negative Cash Conversion
paragraphs: Few Indian industrial companies generate a 37.3% operating margin and 22.2% net margin [1]. Yet per ₹100 of FY26 sales, Azad absorbed ₹50.75 into working capital and non-cash items—turning +₹22.22 of PAT into -₹19.73 of operating cash flow—before spending another ₹94.86 on capex [1]. For the unit economics to become self-funding, H2 FY27 and FY28 must deliver two shifts simultaneously: (1) capex tapering as the 44,800 sq. m. Tuniki Bollaram footprint moves from construction to utilization, and (2) working capital compressing from 304 days [1] toward management's 160–180 day target [6].

web_blocks.title: Cost Structure Shifts: Employee Scale-Up & Interest Friction

web_blocks.html: Standalone cost lines between FY25 and FY26 show how Azad's operating leverage is shifting [14]. Cost of Materials Consumed edged down from ₹62.72 Cr in FY25 to ₹57.04 Cr in FY26. By contrast, Employee Benefits Expense jumped 44% YoY from ₹90.99 Cr to ₹131.02 Cr. Azad hired CNC programmers, metallurgists, and quality engineers ahead of opening the Tuniki Bollaram plants [14]. Other Expenses rose 37% YoY from ₹134.64 Cr to ₹184.56 Cr, driven by power, carbide/diamond tooling, and facility overheads [14]. Those fixed and semi-fixed conversion costs are front-loaded before full plant throughput. Faster Q3–Q4 FY27 billing should lift incremental EBITDA, provided bill-discounting finance costs (₹31 Cr in FY26, ₹41 Cr TTM) do not erode net profit [1][6]. Cash conversion remains the key test for FY27 and FY28. Working capital reached 304 days in FY26 as six new plants stocked raw alloys [1]. Bringing that cycle down toward 160–180 days will determine how fast accounting profits turn into free cash [6].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know whether a precision manufacturer is truly compounding wealth or merely running faster on a capital treadmill, you and I have to follow one hundred rupees of sales all the way from the factory gate to free cash flow. On the surface, Azad Engineering's distribution and supply chain look enviable. There are no middlemen, no regional dealers, and no price wars at the retail counter. Roughly 93 percent of revenue is exported directly to global OEMs under four-to-eight-year Long-Term Contract and Price Agreements. Once Azad qualifies a part and dedicates a bay to MHI, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, or Baker Hughes, purchase orders drop straight from the customer's global scheduling system into Hyderabad.

Why, then, does the cash take so long to arrive? Follow the physical metal. Specialized nickel superalloys and titanium bars are largely imported from OEM-approved mills overseas. They clear customs, sit in quality inspection, enter five-axis machining cells, move through NADCAP heat-treatment and non-destructive testing, and wait for final OEM sign-off before export dispatch. Once shipped, export receivables sit open for 170 to 189 days. In FY26, as Azad stocked raw material and work-in-progress across six newly commissioned plants at Tuniki Bollaram, inventory days spiked to 2,067 days and total working capital days reached 304 days.

Now look at the worked ₹100 waterfall for audited FY26, when consolidated revenue hit ₹603 crore. Out of every ₹100 billed, direct materials consumed only ₹9.46. Employee costs took ₹21.73, and other manufacturing and facility overheads took ₹31.50. That left ₹37.31 of Operating EBITDA—an extraordinary conversion margin for any heavy engineering business. After subtracting ₹8.79 for depreciation, ₹5.14 for interest, adding ₹7.63 of other income, and paying ₹8.79 in taxes, Azad reported ₹22.22 of Net Profit per ₹100 of sales.

Here is where the forensic discipline matters. That ₹22.22 of accounting profit did not become ₹22.22 of cash. Because working capital absorbed ₹50.75 per ₹100 of revenue, Cash Flow from Operations turned negative at minus ₹19.73 per ₹100—an audited outflow of ₹119 crore. On top of that, Azad spent ₹94.86 per ₹100 of revenue—₹572 crore—on capital expenditure to build its dedicated OEM plants, resulting in Free Cash Flow of minus ₹114.59 per ₹100, or minus ₹691 crore in total.

Management is actively trying to break that working-capital logjam using two levers: bill discounting facilities with ICICI Bank and DP World to pull debtor days down toward 90 days, and negotiating 50 percent purchase-order advances with select OEMs. Both help liquidity, though bill discounting shifts some cost back into interest expense. The real test over the next four quarters is simple: as the 44,800 square meters of new Tuniki Bollaram bays finish delta qualification and start shipping at scale, does that minus ₹19.73 operating cash flow flip decisively positive?

Look also at how the cost structure inside that ₹100 waterfall shifted between FY25 and FY26. Direct material consumption actually fell from ₹62.7 crore to ₹57.0 crore, but employee costs surged 44 percent from ₹91.0 crore to ₹131.0 crore as Azad recruited and trained machinists and quality engineers before the new bays even hit full run-rate. Other operating expenses—tooling, power, consumables, and plant overheads—rose 37 percent to ₹184.6 crore. That tells you Azad is carrying the full payroll and utility weight of a much larger factory footprint today; as utilization climbs, fixed-cost absorption should remain a tailwind for margins, even if bill discounting keeps interest costs elevated.

Let us trace that ₹100 FY26 unit-economics waterfall one step further so you see the exact tension between the factory floor and the bank account. Out of every ₹100 Azad billed in FY26, ₹37.31 dropped straight to operating EBITDA, and ₹22.22 survived as reported net profit after depreciation, interest, and taxes. On paper, that looks like an extraordinary industrial machine. Yet when you follow the cash bridge down to the bottom of the waterfall, working-capital absorption and non-cash adjustments wiped out the entire ₹22.22 of net profit and consumed an additional ₹19.73 per ₹100 of sales—leaving operating cash flow at negative ₹19.73 per ₹100 of revenue, before another ₹94.86 per ₹100 went into capital expenditure. That single contrast—+₹22.22 of accounting profit versus -₹114.59 of free cash flow per ₹100 of revenue—is why we audit the cash flow statement before celebrating the P&L.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Never Confuse Gross Margin with Cash Conversion
book_callouts.text: A 37 percent operating margin seduces investors into assuming a business prints cash. Azad's FY26 waterfall proves why you must always trace the bridge from PAT to CFO. When inventory days double to 2,067 and debtor days sit at 189, growth consumes cash instead of generating it—requiring either QIP equity or debt until the new plants hit steady-state turns.

book_callouts.title: MENTAL MODEL: The Bill-Discounting Trade-Off
book_callouts.text: Factoring or discounting export bills with a bank turns a 180-day receivable into cash in days, shrinking debtor days on the balance sheet. But it is not free: the discount fee shows up in finance costs, shaving net margins in exchange for liquidity.

book_subsections.title: Why Six Dedicated OEM Plants Changed the Cost & Working-Capital Equation
paragraphs: When Azad operated primarily out of its legacy Jeedimetla and early Tuniki Bollaram bays, high utilization meant fixed overhead was spread efficiently across steady, mature part numbers. Between 2024 and September 2026, however, Azad commissioned six customer-dedicated plants spanning 44,800 square meters for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Baker Hughes. Think about what happens operationally when you open six specialized factories inside twenty-four months.

First, you must pre-stock exotic nickel and titanium billets well ahead of commercial billing, because lead times on aerospace-grade alloys run six to twelve months. Second, you hire and train specialized CNC programmers, metallurgists, and quality inspectors before those bays reach 80% utilization. Third, export shipments to global OEM hubs incur ocean transit, customs clearance, and customer incoming-quality inspection delays before the 90-to-180-day invoice clock even finishes ticking. That operational sequence—front-loaded raw material, front-loaded labor, and back-ended cash collection—is the exact mechanical reason Azad's FY26 working capital stretched to 304 days.

This is also why the next four quarters are a decisive unit-economics test for Azad. As the six Tuniki Bollaram plants transition from qualification batches into steady-state serial production, the inventory buffer built during FY26 should begin turning faster, while non-recourse export bill discounting should pull debtor days down from 189 days toward management's 90-to-120-day target. When that happens, the ₹100 waterfall will shift from negative operating cash flow back toward self-funding free cash flow—until then, every incremental rupee of revenue remains capital-hungry.
